original_question: Can one develop practical phase-retrieval algorithms, together with window functions and finite sampling schemes in R^d x R^d, such that for every function in a dense subset of L^2(R^d) the reconstruction from finitely many sampled short-time Fourier magnitude measurements converges, up to a global phase factor, to the true function as the number of samples tends to infinity?
target_in_paper: Question 8.9 in Section 8.3 of Section 8, "Problem: Mathematical Foundations of Wigner Distribution Deconvolution."
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official target very closely: it asks for practical phase-retrieval algorithms together with window functions and finite sampling schemes in R^d x R^d, and it requires asymptotic recovery from finitely many sampled short-time Fourier transform magnitudes, up to global phase, for every function in a dense subset of L^2(R^d) as the number of samples tends to infinity.
missing_details: The paper is in the complex-valued infinite-dimensional setting: the object and window are functions f,w : R^d -> C, with w in L^2(R^d).
What is really needed is a family of algorithms indexed by the sample count k, not just an unspecified algorithm.
For each k, the algorithm takes exactly k nonnegative measurements and outputs a function in L^2(R^d): A_k : [0, infinity)^k -> L^2(R^d).
The measurements are specifically squared STFT magnitudes |V_w f|^2 sampled on a finite set, not generic phase-retrieval measurements.
The finite sampling schemes are explicitly of the form Omega_k = {(x_j, xi_j) : 1 <= j <= k} subset R^d x R^d.
The STFT should be defined explicitly: V_w f(x, xi) = integral_{R^d} f(t) w(t - x) e^{-i <t, xi>} dt.
Recovery up to global phase is quantified by inf_{alpha in S^1} ||alpha f - A_k(|V_w f|^2_{Omega_k})||_{L^2(R^d)}, where S^1 = {e^{i theta} : theta in R}.
The quantifier on the recoverable class is existential: the paper asks for convergence for all f in some dense subset of L^2(R^d), not for all of L^2(R^d).
Question 8.9 presents the displayed convergence as an example criterion ("such that, e.g., ..."), so the paper is not asserting that this is the only acceptable formalization.
The paper explicitly notes that the case d > 1 is of particular interest, because the cited approximate finite-sampling results focus on d = 1.
refined_question: For a fixed dimension d >= 1, can one construct a window w in L^2(R^d), finite sampling sets Omega_k = {(x_j, xi_j) : 1 <= j <= k} subset R^d x R^d, and a family of practical phase-retrieval algorithms A_k : [0, infinity)^k -> L^2(R^d) such that, if V_w f(x, xi) = integral_{R^d} f(t) w(t - x)e^{-i <t, xi>} dt and y_k(f) = (|V_w f(x_j, xi_j)|^2)_{j=1}^k, then, for example, inf_{alpha in S^1} ||alpha f - A_k(y_k(f))||_{L^2(R^d)} -> 0 as k -> infinity for every f in some dense subset of L^2(R^d), especially in the higher-dimensional case d > 1?
justification: The draft is targeting Question 8.9 almost verbatim. The decisive features are the demand for practical algorithms, finite sampling schemes Omega_k subset R^d x R^d, reconstruction from finitely many sampled STFT magnitudes, convergence as k -> infinity, and recovery only on a dense subset of L^2(R^d); these are exactly the ingredients of Question 8.9 in Section 8.3. The nearby context in Section 8.3 defines sampled STFT phase retrieval and the global-phase equivalence relation, then explains that recovering all of L^2(R) from lattice STFT or Gabor data is impossible and discusses a weaker dense-set question for infinite Gabor sampling. The summary paragraph immediately before Question 8.9 says that only the cited works [61, 94] treat approximate recovery from finite measurement sets, which is precisely why Question 8.9 asks for finite-sample algorithms with asymptotic convergence on a dense set rather than a uniqueness theorem for all signals. Questions 8.6-8.8 are neighboring problems about admissible windows, informative infinite sampling sets, and dense recoverable sets on Gabor lattices, but your draft is most closely aligned with Question 8.9.
